title: Check: what Kubernetes is
description: Five questions on orchestration, the declarative model and the reconciliation loop.

questions.prompt: Containers solved packaging. Which problem did they NOT solve?

options.text: Bundling an application with its dependencies
Restarting workloads when the node running them dies
Producing an image that runs the same in CI and production
Isolating one process from another on the same host

questions.explanation: Packaging is exactly what a container image solves. What happens after `docker run` - restarts, rescheduling, rollouts, service discovery - is what orchestration adds.

questions.prompt: What is the defining difference between a declarative and an imperative system?

options.text: Declarative systems are written in YAML, imperative ones in JSON
A declarative system stores the desired outcome and keeps working to match it
An imperative system is always faster
A declarative system runs commands in a fixed order

questions.explanation: An imperative system carries out an order once. A declarative one stores a description of the outcome and works forever to make reality match it - which is why a deleted Pod comes back.

questions.prompt: A Deployment declares `replicas: 3` and you delete one of its Pods. What happens?

options.text: Nothing - the order to create three Pods was already carried out
A controller notices the gap and creates a replacement
The Deployment is marked failed until you re-apply it
The remaining two Pods are restarted

questions.explanation: `replicas: 3` is desired state, not a one-off instruction. A controller sees two where three should be and closes the gap without you writing 'restart it' anywhere.

questions.prompt: Which of these follow from the reconciliation loop? Choose all that apply.

options.text: A drained node's Pods are recreated elsewhere
A container that exits is restarted
Every change must be applied twice to take effect
The cluster converges on the state you declared

questions.explanation: Reconciliation means a controller continuously drives the cluster toward the declared state. Nothing about it requires applying a change twice.

questions.prompt: The lesson suggests a habit for exam questions. What is it?

options.text: Reach for `kubectl edit` first
Ask what the desired state is, then make a small YAML change and apply it
Restart the kubelet before changing anything
Always delete and recreate the object

questions.explanation: Re-read the question and ask 'what is the desired state?' The answer is almost always a small YAML change plus `kubectl apply`, not a sequence of manual steps.
